title: How to Use TIPS (Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities) for Retirement Security
description: The mechanics of the government bond that guarantees your purchasing power.
content:
Inflation is the enemy of the retiree. A standard bond paying 4% loses money in real terms if inflation is 5%. To protect your standard of living over a 30-year retirement, you need assets that adjust automatically to the cost of living. Enter **TIPS** (Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities). These are US government bonds where the principal value rises with the Consumer Price Index (CPI). They are the only asset class that guarantees a 'Real Return' above inflation, making them a cornerstone of a defensive retirement portfolio.

Key Takeaways

  • The Inflation Adjustment: Unlike regular bonds where the coupon is fixed, TIPS adjust their principal value every 6 months based on CPI. If inflation spikes, your bond value spikes.
  • Real Yield: TIPS are quoted in 'Real Yield'. If a TIPS bond pays 1.5%, that means it pays 1.5% above inflation. If inflation is 3%, your total return is roughly 4.5%.
  • The 'Phantom Tax' Problem: The IRS taxes the inflation adjustment in the year it occurs, even though you don't receive the cash until maturity. This makes TIPS messy in taxable accounts. Ideally, hold them in an IRA.
  • Duration Risk: TIPS are still bonds. If interest rates rise, the market price of a TIPS ETF can fall, even if inflation is high. Holding individual bonds to maturity eliminates this price risk.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Social Security is an inflation-indexed annuity. TIPS are an inflation-indexed asset. Combining them creates a 'Floor' of purchasing power that protects you from 1970s-style stagflation.

How TIPS Work

Scenario: You buy $10,000 of TIPS with a 1% coupon.

Year 1: Low Inflation

Inflation is 2%.
Principal Adjustment: $10,000 becomes $10,200.
Interest Payment: 1% of $10,200 = $102.

Year 2: High Inflation

Inflation jumps to 8%.
Principal Adjustment: $10,200 becomes $11,016.
Interest Payment: 1% of $11,016 = $110.
Result: Both your asset value and your income check grew. A standard bond would have lost massive value in this scenario.

The Deflation Floor

If deflation occurs (prices drop), the principal adjusts down. However, the US Treasury guarantees you will never get back less than the original par value at maturity. It is a heads-I-win, tails-I-don't-lose proposition.

Implementation Guide

  1. Asset Location: Always put TIPS in a Tax-Deferred account (Traditional IRA/401k). This avoids the headache of paying taxes on 'Phantom Income' (the principal adjustment) that you haven't received yet.
  2. TIPS Ladder: Build a ladder of individual TIPS bonds maturing in 2026, 2027, 2028, etc. This guarantees a stream of inflation-adjusted cash flow for spending.
  3. The ETF Route: For simplicity, buy **VTIP** (Short-Term TIPS) or **SCHP** (Broad TIPS). Note that ETFs don't have a maturity date, so their price fluctuates. Short-term ETFs (VTIP) are less volatile.
  4. Allocation: Consider replacing 20-30% of your nominal bond allocation (BND) with TIPS. This diversifies your inflation risk without sacrificing safety.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did TIPS lose money in 2022?

Inflation was high (good for TIPS), but interest rates rose faster (bad for bonds). The price drop from rising rates outweighed the inflation adjustment. Individual TIPS held to maturity did not lose money; only the ETFs showed a paper loss.

Are I-Bonds better?

I-Bonds are simpler (no interest rate risk, tax-deferred) but have a $10k annual limit. TIPS have no purchase limit. Use I-Bonds first, then spill over into TIPS.

Is Gold better?

Gold is a speculative hedge. TIPS are a mathematical hedge. TIPS guarantee a real return; Gold guarantees nothing. TIPS are safer for retirees.
